paragraphs: We have already reported, in Maqāla I, the position of Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī on ketib and qere: he denied them and claimed they were "conventions" (awḍāʿ) invented by certain people for profit, holding that the reading must conform to the written form. We noted that his position is self-contradicting, since he also said there are things in Scripture that have been altered (which is the very opposite claim). Some of the Khurasani [Rabbanite] groups have made a partial version of the same claim only with respect to the Tetragrammaton: they hold that it must be pronounced as written — YHWH — and that whoever reads it differently has opposed God and belittled His name. They argue from Isa 64:6, "and there is none that calleth on Thy name" — taking the verse as a prophetic complaint against the Diaspora, who do not pronounce the divine name in its true form. They also cite Isa 65:1, "I said: Behold Me, behold Me, unto a nation that was not called by My name" — was not called meaning does not call. And his own Holy name (Cairo l. 5149) […].

What we have just demonstrated, regarding the soundness of the Torah-text by naql that admits no impeachment, refutes this position. For the agreement of the entire community, East to West, on the reading — is on a par with the agreement on the soundness of the text itself: no addition, no deletion. Likewise they are agreed, for example, that what is written yiyaʿar / yishakhev in Isa 13:16 / Deut 28:30 is to be read yishkav, that what is written naʿărā (defective) at Deut 22:23ff. is to be read naʿărā (with qamatz), and so on for all the cases — without dispute, and without ascription to specific individuals (whether Rabbanite or non-Rabbanite).

For the divine name itself, the matter is even more strongly settled. The Rabbanites themselves claim that whoever reads the Tetragrammaton as it is written has committed kufr and is liable to death — quoting Lev 24:16, "and he that blasphemeth the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death," and reading "blaspheme" (niqqēv) as "pronounce the Tetragrammaton as written." We need not endorse the Rabbanite exegesis to use the point: what we want to show is that there is no one in the community who reads the Tetragrammaton as it is written. The fact of universal abstinence proves the universality of the qere-tradition.

If the recitation could have been altered, by the entire community from East to West abandoning the original — or if the community could have read things that are not written — then by the same principle, the original text could have been altered. The Rabbanites did not in fact accomplish this with respect to the text; we find numerous naṣṣ-passages that contradict their aḥkām still intact in the text. They could not alter these, since the text was distributed throughout the world. The fact that they did not alter the text demonstrates their inability to alter even the reading, which is held by the same broad community.

Some of our companions hold that God Himself (mighty and exalted) is the guardian of the text. They cite David: when he describes [the situation], he says (Ps 12:2), "help, Lord, for the godly man ceaseth"; he then says (v. 7), "the words of the Lord are pure words; as silver tried in a furnace upon the earth, refined seven times" — and (v. 8), "thou wilt keep them, O Lord." David's claim is that God Himself preserves Scripture from the kind of alteration and substitution we have noted.

Our companions have also rebutted al-ʿUkbarī's claim that the reading must conform to the writing. They have shown: Ps 119:166 ("sibbarti, I hoped, [for Thy salvation]") is written with a sin but must be read "shibbarti" — for shibbarti with the standard shin would mean "I shattered," which makes no sense in context. Likewise Ps 119:162 ("sas anokhi, I rejoice") must be read with sin, not samekh — for with samekh it would mean "six" (shesh). Likewise shoṭerīm ("officers") must be read with shin — not sin, which would yield a different sense. Every defective writing of naʿărāh must be read as a feminine noun and not a masculine, since otherwise it would mean "boy" (naʿar) and the verse would be unintelligible.[{2}] There are many cases of this kind: read literally according to the writing, the sense breaks down completely.

Whoever does not return, in his reading and recitation, to what the community has fixed by naql — can establish no reading at all, and no word securely. There is no word that cannot be vocalized in multiple ways: the very first word of the Torah, bereshit, can be vocalized variously: with qamatz (long a), with fatḥa (short a), or with shewa (silent); the aleph can be dropped from the vocalization or kept in; there are many other vocalization-possibilities. The same holds for every word in the language, down to two-letter particles: kī ("for"), naʾ ("please, now") — each can be vocalized in multiple ways analogous to those of bereshit. If the ijmāʿ of the community on reading-and-recitation is not probative, by what means do we determine which of these vocalizations is correct? Indeed: if the correct vocalization is what the community has read, and if the community has read in ways diverging from the written form, then the qere differing from the ketib is the correct vocalization — exactly as transmitted from the era of the prophets to the present. The same applies to the holders of the position that the Tetragrammaton must be read as written: they too must rely on the community's vocalization to know how to pronounce the yod-he-vav-he — since the consonants alone do not fix the vocalization.

Likewise, the various biblical references to the acts of God depend on community-vocalization to be readable at all. The first word at Exod 15:1, 21 ("ki gaʾoh gaʾah"), is not readable in plain consonants. The various conjunctive waw-particles, the demonstrative zū vs zeh, the verbal forms kān, bēn, yad, lahem, ʿasah — all require community-vocalization tradition. This concludes our reply to Ismaʿīl al-ʿUkbarī and to anyone else who invalidates ketib-and-qere.
As to what he claimed: that in the Book there are things that have dropped out, that scribes erred in […].[{3}] ---
